frase_gancho.texto: A sculpture carved from a wood so hard that it sinks in water.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the wood of the coast we move on to the sierra. Look for a mural by the painter Pablo O’Higgins, born in the United States, whose title mentions the Sierra Tarahumara, the land of the Rarámuri (Tarahumara).

guion_corto.texto: This sculpture is carved from ironwood, a wood so hard and heavy that if you toss it into the water, it sinks. It is the tree of the Sonora desert, and Seri artisans from Punta Chueca and El Desemboque work it with machetes, files, and sandpaper. After polishing the piece, they rub it with wax until it has a soft shine that brings out the grain: the dark, almost black heartwood, and the lighter parts of the wood. What you see is the stylized silhouette of an animal, and that is typical: the Seri carve turtles, sharks, whales, sea lions, and bighorn sheep, creatures with whom they share their territory. For them these are not just decorations: they express respect for the animals of the sea and the desert.

guion_largo.texto:
A desert tree does a great deal for others. In the shade of the ironwood, small cacti and other plants sprout, and that is why biologists call it a “nurse tree.” It grows slowly and lives for centuries: some specimens are hundreds of years old. Its wood is one of the densest in existence, so heavy that it does not float, and so hard that it cannot be carved with a knife, only with strong tools.

Punta Chueca lies across from the Infiernillo Channel, the strait that separates it from Tiburón Island, and the sculptors work with the sea in view. The tradition of sculpting ironwood is younger than it seems. It is usually placed in the second half of the twentieth century, when Seri artisans began to carve animals with simple tools. In just a few decades it became one of the most recognized arts of the Northwest, and today it is a living tradition, with master artists from several generations.

Look at how the wood is put to use. The center of the trunk is almost black, and the outer part, the sapwood, is light. The sculptor uses these contrasts: the dark defines the back or the shell, and the light, the fins, the head, or the belly. It is as if the tree came with two colors of paint already in it, and the artist only had to draw with form.

Polishing is the slowest part. The piece is carved with a machete, refined with a rasp and files, sanded again and again, and finally rubbed with wax to bring out the shine. If you run your hand over a piece like this, the surface feels as smooth as a river stone. That smoothness is the result of hours and hours of patience.

The animals are no accident. The Seri carve loggerhead turtles, sharks, whales, and sea lions, and also bighorn sheep, which live in the desert and on the islands. They are the neighbors of the territory, and carving them is a way of showing respect for those who share the water and the sand. The [coritas](mna_s20_corita_seri) basket you saw a moment ago and this sculpture are, in this way, two portraits of the same world.

Because ironwood grows very slowly, a large sculpture comes from a tree that took many years to grow, and its use has worried ecologists; there has been debate about how to use it without harming the desert woodlands. It is a current question for the sculptors: how to make a living from the tree without losing it. Those who know it best are, precisely, the ones who have cared for it for generations.

For many Comcaac (Seri) families, these sculptures are also a source of income, along with the baskets. It is not just art: it is the work with which they buy what they need to live. They deserve to be viewed with that respect, as a craft and not as an ornament.

Up to here you have seen four paths: the mask, the violin, the spiral, and the wood. In each one, a people take what they have at hand, leather, pine, torote, ironwood, and give it meaning. It is a lesson from the Northwest: in a harsh land, beauty is also a way of resisting. Two more stops still await you in this hall: a painting of the sierra and a dance.

texto.Region: Coast of the Sonoran Desert (Punta Chueca and Desemboque, Sonora)
texto.Technique/Material: Inert ironwood (Olneya tesota), hand-carved, sanded and burnished with wax

texto.respuesta: Reality: Ironwood is so dense that it sinks in water. The Seri carve it to represent animals of their territory.
